items.prompt: In most interview languages, concatenating two strings of length n and m typically costs what?
choices: O(n + m) because a new buffer is allocated and filled
O(1) because strings are mutable in place
O(log(n + m)) from a balanced tree
O(n · m) from nested character compares
items.whyRight: Immutable or copy-on-write strings build a new sequence, so work tracks the output length.
whyWrong: In-place mutation is not the default for interview string APIs; edits usually allocate.
Logarithmic cost is not how flat string concatenation is priced.
Nested compares describe matching algorithms, not building a concatenation.

items.prompt: You need the character at index i of a string stored as a contiguous buffer. Typical cost?
choices: O(i)
O(n)
O(log n)
items.whyRight: Like an array, index i is base address plus offset.
whyWrong: Walking i characters is a linked representation, not a contiguous buffer.
Full length only matters if you scan; a direct index does not.
Binary search is unrelated to a plain index read.

items.prompt: Why is building a long string by repeatedly doing s = s + ch in a loop often quadratic?
choices: Each append may copy the growing prefix again
Character comparison is always quadratic
The hash of the string doubles each time
The runtime inserts a sort after every append
items.whyRight: If each concatenation copies the whole current string, total work is 1+2+…+n.
whyWrong: Comparing characters is not required just to append.
Hashing is not the driver of naive concatenation cost.
Sorts are not inserted by the language on append.

items.prompt: A problem asks whether two strings are anagrams. Which structure usually makes the check linear?
choices: A count map (or fixed alphabet array) of character frequencies
A balanced BST of every substring
Sorting both strings is impossible to beat
A graph of character edges
items.whyRight: One pass builds counts; another compares them — O(n) for fixed alphabets.
whyWrong: Substring trees are heavier than needed for anagram equality.
Sorting works in n log n but is not the only or best typical answer.
Graphs do not model anagram counts.

items.prompt: You must reverse a string in place in an interview language that exposes a mutable buffer. Best approach?
choices: Two pointers from both ends swapping toward the middle
Recursively allocate a new string each call
Insert each character at the front of a linked list of chars
Sort the characters descending
items.whyRight: Swaps from the ends reverse with O(1) extra space and one pass.
whyWrong: Fresh allocation per call wastes space and is not in-place.
A list of characters adds pointer overhead without helping reverse.
Sorting changes order by value, not by reverse position.

items.prompt: Unicode-aware length vs code-unit length trips candidates. What should you say first?
choices: Ask whether the interviewer means code points, graphemes, or UTF-16/UTF-8 units
Always report strlen of raw bytes as character count
Assume ASCII forever
Claim strings have no length
items.whyRight: Interview prompts often hide encoding; clarifying the unit prevents wrong off-by-ones.
whyWrong: Raw byte length is not always what “character” means.
ASCII-only is an unsafe silent assumption.
Strings have measurable length; the dispute is the unit.
